![Image from [Citrini Research](https://www.citriniresearch.com/p/2028gic).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

In late February 2026, two finance-side pieces on AI-driven labor displacement came out within two days of each other. On February 22, Citrini Research [[1]](#ref-1), co-authored with Alap Shah of LOTUS Investment Management, imagined a "2028 Global Intelligence Crisis" in which recursive AI capability and the substitution of labor costs with compute costs crater the economy by 2028. On February 24, Citadel Securities [[2]](#ref-2) published a direct rebuttal: the data is not showing the inflection, and even the strong-substitution scenario does not automatically produce a macro contraction. The two pieces share a mechanism and disagree on where we currently sit on the adoption curve.

## The scenario (Citrini Research, Feb 22, 2026)

Citrini [[1]](#ref-1) describes the piece as a thought exercise rather than a forecast:

> What if our AI bullishness continues to be right...and what if that's actually bearish?

The piece is written as a fictional report from June 2028, looking back on how AI replacing white-collar workers produced a market crash and a sharp rise in unemployment. What it imagines:

- **The setup (late 2025 through 2026).** By late 2025, AI coding tools are good enough that a single engineer with Claude Code or Codex can rebuild the core of a standard business-software product in weeks. Mid-2026 is the first time large-company buying decisions are made with that knowledge. When ServiceNow posts sharply slowing growth alongside a round of layoffs, the self-reinforcing loop becomes visible in public data: companies cut staff, redirect the savings into more AI tools, and those same tools put pressure on the vendors selling them.
- **Agents take over everyday commerce (early 2027).** AI agents start doing the tedious shopping work humans used to do: canceling forgotten subscriptions, re-shopping insurance at renewal, comparing travel prices across booking sites, driving real-estate commissions for buyers toward a fraction of the old rate. On Mastercard's first earnings call of 2027, management names "agent-led price optimization" as the reason card spending is slowing. Agents also skip card networks entirely, settling in digital dollars on faster blockchains for a tiny fraction of the usual cost. Businesses that made money from customer inertia and friction see their revenue compress.
- **How this hits the broader economy.** The US economy runs on non-essential spending by high earners, with the top tenth of earners accounting for more than half of all consumer spending. If the layoffs concentrate in white-collar work, the spending hit is much larger than the raw unemployment number suggests. The authors coin "Ghost GDP" for economic output that shows up in official statistics but never cycles back through household spending. Labor's share of economic output, already falling since the 1970s, drops to its steepest low on record.
- **The private-credit unwind.** In autumn 2027, Zendesk defaults on the largest loan ever backed by software-subscription revenue, a multi-billion-dollar private loan from its private-equity buyout years earlier. Private-credit managers had promised their capital was safe because it was locked up for a decade or more. Most of that capital turns out to be retirees' annuity savings (annuities are retirement products where you pay an insurer now and it pays you back over time), held through life insurers that private-equity firms quietly bought over the previous decade and routed through offshore affiliates. When the software loans go bad, the losses land on those retirees.
- **The mortgage hit.** By mid-2028, home prices fall across the tech-heavy metros. Fannie Mae flags early signs of missed payments in ZIP codes where tech and finance jobs dominate. The US mortgage market assumes borrowers will keep earning roughly what they earn today for the thirty-year life of the loan. The authors' summary: in 2008, the loans were bad on day one; in 2028, they were fine on day one and the world changed out from under them.
- **The policy response.** Federal tax receipts come in well below the budget office's projection because income and payroll taxes are, in effect, a tax on paid human work. Automatic unemployment benefits were designed for an ordinary recession, not a permanent job loss from a technology shift. Congress debates two bills: a "Transition Economy Act" funded by deficit spending and a tax on AI processing, and a more radical "Shared AI Prosperity Act" that would set up a public stake in AI output with dividends funding household transfers. Both stall in partisan fights. Protesters blockade the Anthropic and OpenAI offices in San Francisco for weeks. The authors close: "You're reading it in February 2026... The canary is still alive."

## The rebuttal (Citadel Securities, Feb 24, 2026)

Citadel [[2]](#ref-2) answers with its thesis in a single line:

> Recursive capability does not imply recursive adoption.

Two days after Citrini's piece, Citadel Securities published a market-insights note arguing that the displacement narrative is ahead of any empirical inflection, and that even the strong-substitution scenario does not automatically produce a macro contraction. What the note argues:

- **The macro snapshot.** US unemployment at 4.28% [[3]](#ref-3), AI capital spending at roughly 2% of GDP ($650bn), AI-adjacent commodities up 65% since January 2023, about 2,800 US data centers planned [[4]](#ref-4). Despite the displacement narrative, job postings for software engineers are up 11% year-on-year [[5]](#ref-5).
- **Adoption isn't inflecting.** Intensive daily use of generative AI at work, as measured by the St Louis Fed's Real-Time Population Survey (RTPS) [[6]](#ref-6), has been "unexpectedly stable" rather than climbing. The binary question ("do you use AI?") looks different from the question that actually matters for displacement ("how intensely, for work?"), and the intensive-use series is flat.
- **Adoption lags capability.** Technological diffusion follows an S-curve; the AI debate conflates what the technology can do with how fast the economy actually deploys it. Organizational integration is costly, regulation emerges, and returns to the next marginal deployment decline. Markets extrapolate the acceleration phase linearly and miss the plateau.
- **Compute sets a soft ceiling.** Displacing white-collar labor at scale would require orders of magnitude more compute than current utilization. Rapid displacement drives compute demand up and compute's marginal cost with it. Once compute for a given task costs more than the human doing that task, substitution stops being worthwhile, and further displacement slows.
- **Productivity shocks are supply shocks.** AI-driven automation is a productivity shock, and productivity shocks are positive supply shocks. When firms produce more for less, either prices fall or margins widen. Lower prices raise real purchasing power, which lifts household consumption. Wider margins raise retained earnings, which lifts business investment. GDP is the sum of consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. If the productivity shock raises GDP, at least one of those four has to rise with it. For AI to cut aggregate demand while raising output, all four channels would have to fail at once, and elected governments would have to take no offsetting action as white-collar unemployment climbs. Every prior technological wave (steam, electrification, the internal combustion engine, computing) has fit the supply-shock pattern.
- **The complement case.** Cognitive automation runs into coordination frictions, liability constraints, and trust barriers that keep even mature productivity tools from collapsing labor demand. When Microsoft Office arrived, the worry was that it would replace office workers. In practice it complemented them, altering the composition of tasks rather than eliminating labor.
- **New business formation is rising.** US new-business applications have roughly doubled since 2019 [[7]](#ref-7), and the forward-looking components of Citadel's own labor-market tracker are improving. AI data-center construction is itself driving a pickup in construction hiring. If AI were already displacing labor at the pace the displacement narrative assumes, the payroll and business-formation data would look very different.
- **The Keynes analogy.** Keynes predicted in 1930 [[8]](#ref-8) that productivity would drive the workweek down to fifteen hours. Productivity rose as he expected. Hours did not fall. Consumption expanded instead: falling prices let people buy more, and new industries kept creating new things to want. Citadel runs the same argument forward. If human wants remain elastic, AI-driven productivity gains lower prices and seed new industries rather than collapsing demand. Advanced-economy trend growth has sat near 2% through every prior wave. AI, Citadel concludes, may be just enough to offset the secular headwinds from ageing populations, deglobalization, and climate transition.

## My Notes

- **An empirical dispute, short horizon.** Citrini and Citadel accept the same underlying mechanism and disagree only on whether AI adoption is inflecting now or still flat.
- **What the data shows through today.** Three months after the exchange, the aggregate labor and business data still sit where Citadel described them: unemployment in the low 4s, new-business applications elevated [[7]](#ref-7), software-engineer job postings rising, and RTPS intensive-use flat [[6]](#ref-6). The claims Citrini's scenario dates to 2026–2027 (visible card-network and subscription-revenue compression from agent-led commerce, a bellwether SaaS vendor posting a growth-and-layoffs step-change) are either just beginning or not yet showing in public earnings. Neither side has been falsified. Citadel's reading fits what the data shows through today; Citrini's predictions are dated to periods still ahead.
- **Citrini overlooks the human-plus-AI pattern.** Citrini assumes no natural brake on displacement. But the [Anthropic Economic Index](/posts/20260423-anthropic-economic-index/) finds that the most productive AI work today is humans directing AI rather than AI replacing humans at a task. That's a pattern where AI adoption grows without eliminating workers, and the scenario doesn't account for it. The complement framing isn't new either: [Steve Miller and Tom Davenport made the same case in 2022](/posts/20230203-ai-job-automation-augmentation/#ch-augmentation-vs-automation), with 29 case studies in which AI deployment was augmentation rather than automation.
- **Citadel's compute ceiling is already dropping.** Citadel says today's compute is too expensive to displace labor at scale. But the 2,800 planned US data centers it cites as evidence of investment strength are adding supply, and inference cost for GPT-3.5-level performance dropped more than 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024 [[9]](#ref-9). Hardware cost fell 30% annually over that stretch and energy efficiency rose 40% annually. Each of these trends weakens Citadel's claim that compute cost makes large-scale displacement too expensive.
- **The Jevons Paradox.** When William Stanley Jevons studied coal use in 1865 [[10]](#ref-10), he found that Watt's more efficient steam engine raised coal consumption rather than lowering it: cheaper energy opened new uses faster than efficiency could compensate. Applied to AI: falling inference cost expands the set of tasks worth running models on, which raises total compute demand even as per-unit cost drops. That weakens Citadel's compute-cost argument against displacement, but doesn't validate Citrini's scenario either: rising AI usage could still be complement rather than substitute, which is what Citadel's own Microsoft-Office point allows.
- **Where the Keynes analogy breaks.** Citadel leans on Keynes's elasticity-of-wants argument against sustained demand collapse, but that move assumes the work to satisfy expanding wants stays human-doable, which is exactly what AI displacement puts in question. The analogy holds only if cognitive work resists automation the way office work and physical work did in prior waves.
- **Agent commerce is testable now.** If AI agents are genuinely canceling idle subscriptions, re-shopping insurance, aggregating travel, and compressing real-estate commissions, those effects surface in public-market revenue reports well before 2028. The cleanest near-term signal is revenue growth and transaction volume slowing together at the payments networks, booking sites, and marketplaces Citrini names.
